Washington is gripped by an artificial intelligence (AI) panic, driven by the prospect of superintelligent models delivering our doom. Today’s Nostradamuses include whistleblowers from frontier AI companies—who put the odds of AI killing all humans at greater than one in 10 and warn that insiders expect it could happen before the end of the decade—and anti-nuclear activists, who note that it wouldn’t be the first time humanity built something that could kill us all. The doomsayers may yet be right, but their scenario rests on a long chain of assumptions, each highly unlikely on its own and far less likely to align all at once.

This doesn’t mean AI isn’t dangerous. But by fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios, we miss the forest for the trees: the common, mundane AI dangers already present and actively causing harm. The pressing AI risk Washington should focus on more is automation bias, the phenomenon where humans over-rely on or over-delegate to AI relative to the accuracy of AI models, off-loading cognition to the machine, sometimes even in the face of contradictory evidence.

Washington is gripped by an artificial intelligence (AI) panic, driven by the prospect of superintelligent models delivering our doom. Today’s Nostradamuses include whistleblowers from frontier AI companies—who put the odds of AI killing all humans at greater than one in 10 and warn that insiders expect it could happen before the end of the decade—and anti-nuclear activists, who note that it wouldn’t be the first time humanity built something that could kill us all. The doomsayers may yet be right, but their scenario rests on a long chain of assumptions, each highly unlikely on its own and far less likely to align all at once.

This doesn’t mean AI isn’t dangerous. But by fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios, we miss the forest for the trees: the common, mundane AI dangers already present and actively causing harm. The pressing AI risk Washington should focus on more is automation bias, the phenomenon where humans over-rely on or over-delegate to AI relative to the accuracy of AI models, off-loading cognition to the machine, sometimes even in the face of contradictory evidence.

The high-profile insistence on AI safety to address the risk of extinction from AI superweapons created by the most advanced large language models (LLMs) distracts attention from the urgent risks we should and can begin to solve now: human errors in operational usage of AI today due to automation bias.

A Chinese-flagged container ship transits the Gulf of Oman on Oct. 13. AFP via Getty Images

This spring, during the U.S. war with Iran, it appears that an intelligence report suggested that China was sending nuclear weapons components on a ship in the Middle East toward Iran. The U.S. military immediately began surveillance and made plans to intercept and board the vessel. Just before the operation began, officials reexamined the original report. They discovered it came from an analyst who forwarded an AI model’s output that stitched together intelligence to suggest the ship carried nuclear components. The report was false, with the AI model either incorrectly identifying or hallucinating the nature of the vessel’s cargo.

It’s easy to blame the AI for the false report. But what matters more is that the analyst didn’t check what the model had generated, and neither did the planners who received the report. The analyst entered the fabricated AI claim into a standard intelligence report that went up the chain of command, and no one checked until it was almost too late. Better AI or guardrails on AI models would not have solved the problem.

For those who know their Cold War history, this should ring alarm bells. In September 1983, Soviet early-warning satellites reported that the United States had launched nuclear missiles. The duty officer, Stanislav Petrov, judged it a false alarm and declined to report it up the chain as an attack. He was right, and he likely averted nuclear war. This spring’s episode was, in essence, a Petrov incident without a Petrov. In 1983, a machine raised a false alarm and a human had the presence of mind to question it. This time, a machine raised a false alarm, and the human analyst passed it along. The error surfaced only on a last-minute second look.

It’s evident to anyone how close of a call this was, and how near to danger we came. Sen. Mark Warner recently stated that for Congress to take real action, we will need a “holy heck moment.” This near-miss incident probably won’t qualify—it drew a fraction of the attention and news coverage given to this summer’s Hugging Face incident, in which OpenAI models escaped their testing environment and breached the company’s servers—but it should. The episode did not go unnoticed, on the other hand, in China, where one news outlet described the failure as one wherein the machine “merely handed over a crooked ruler,” but humans were the ones who ultimately did the measuring.

Talk of “super intelligence” distracts from frequent screwups.

Beijing has a strategy. Washington has a voluntary pledge and a “Super Intelligence Force.”

Just as British people did with steam power, the American public can shape how this technology spreads.

The near-miss regarding the Chinese ship is not the only example. Airline pilots fall prey to automation bias when they ignore their instruments and training and trust the autopilot too much, causing tragic plane crashes that have killed hundreds over the past three decades. Automation bias in drivers occurs when navigation software routes them onto a closed road (as in the famous Allstate commercial); instead of using their eyes and judgment, they follow it anyway. For the military, a classic example happened in 2003, when Patriot missile systems in Iraq classified friendly aircraft as incoming missiles, and operators approved engagements that killed British and American troops.

Despite its prevalence today, this type of human error does not feature heavily in the AI argument now consuming Washington. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing frontier development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warns that humanity could lose control of AI, while U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the push for restrictions as a “conspiracy.” The current debate focuses on guardrails for what labs build and the potential for doomsday scenarios. One explanation for the focus on doomsday scenarios is that      they capture the public imagination. Another is that they distract from the complicated reasons that real-world accidents often occur. Accidents regularly result from the interactions among people, organizations, and technologies. The tendency in the non-AI accident realm (think a plane crash) is to blame the pilot, rather than the complex system and interaction among the pilot, their training, and the technology that leads to the accident. We could be seeing the AI version of that dynamic, where the AI becomes the scapegoat.

But the near-miss with the Chinese ship shows what can happen if we continue to ignore the risks with AI systems that already exist and are already being (mis)used.

In January, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released an Artificial Intelligence Acceleration Strategy designed to put AI tools in the hands of 3 million military and civilian personnel at every classification level. Scaling AI adoption is essential to U.S. military power, but it must happen responsibly to be effective. The new strategy emphasizes expanding access to data, compute, and AI tools from warfighting to intelligence to enterprise, and even special hiring authorities for AI talent. The next step, conspicuously missing from the AI Acceleration Strategy, is training to ensure commanders and operators understand the advantages and risks of the AI systems they use.

Automation bias is not inevitable, and if the American government, including but not limited to the military, can address it, the United States can lead the world in AI adoption with responsible speed. Based on our experience working in the Pentagon and doing research on practical AI risks, two changes would help the United States capture the benefits of AI and mitigate much of the risk.

U.S. Army cadets take notes during a lecture on terrorism at the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York, on March 30, 2007. Don Emmert/AFP via Getty Images

First, create standard operating procedures for managing AI outputs. For example, any finished intelligence product that used a generative AI tool should say so, visibly, to everyone who reads it. The analyst in this recent incident reportedly used AI to both query intelligence reports and then to package the findings, and in this final report failed to disclose AI use, making the report’s content look human-generated. Furthermore, AI inferences in intelligence reports should require confirmation beyond the AI model for high-risk decisions. Boarding a Chinese vessel during an ongoing war would have been incredibly risky. Speed that leads to operational failure isn’t useful. One additional operational check can make a huge difference without substantially slowing things down. This does not only apply to intelligence products, though there is a unique risk there—but also to any output aided by AI tools, including in the use of AI decision-support systems.

The second is training. In co-authored research, we found that people with the least experience with AI models were the most likely to defer to them, a version of the Dunning-Kruger effect applied to machines. Familiarity built through structured training, including exposure to these systems failing, produces better, more effective AI users. In more recent work, we found that West Point cadets exhibited automation bias in 3.9 percent of trials, compared with 9 percent in a matched sample of the American public, suggesting that military education can help produce personnel who interrogate algorithmic outputs to maximize their effective usage instead of merely accepting them.

The danger of automation bias will not be engineered away by better models or models that never hallucinate, because the failure comes from how people use them. The military is not helpless here. Solving AI risk is more about people and organizations than engineering, and it’s not an imagined problem for tomorrow.

Michael C. Horowitz is the director of Perry World House and the Richard Perry professor at the University of Pennsylvania, and a senior fellow for technology and innovation at the Council on Foreign Relations. X: @mchorowitz

Lauren Kahn is a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

Analysis: Reigniting War With Iran Would Be a ‘Huge Gamble’

Growing signs suggest that U.S. President Donald Trump could restart the war with Iran following the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.

While there have been renewed diplomatic efforts to reach a deal over the past week, the terms Iran has put on the table—including lifting all U.S. sanctions—would be difficult for the United States to accept. Meanwhile, Trump has offered mixed signals on what he plans to do, indicating that he hasn’t yet made a decision. Over the weekend, Trump said the war could be over soon, but he also said that the U.S. still had to “take care” of one or two nuclear sites and would have to give Iran “the hammer” at some point.

Growing signs suggest that U.S. President Donald Trump could restart the war with Iran following the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.

While there have been renewed diplomatic efforts to reach a deal over the past week, the terms Iran has put on the table—including lifting all U.S. sanctions—would be difficult for the United States to accept. Meanwhile, Trump has offered mixed signals on what he plans to do, indicating that he hasn’t yet made a decision. Over the weekend, Trump said the war could be over soon, but he also said that the U.S. still had to “take care” of one or two nuclear sites and would have to give Iran “the hammer” at some point.

The war has cost U.S. taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion so far and has left the United States military depleted on a number of levels—from drastically reducing key munitions stockpiles to the destruction of expensive equipment and aircraft.

The U.S. is estimated to have used up to 65 percent of its Patriot air-defense interceptors and 80 percent of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) ballistic missile interceptors since the war began, for example. The U.S. stockpile of Tomahawk cruise missiles is estimated to have fallen from around 3,000 to 2,000 since the fighting started, and the war has reportedly left its stocks of missiles for the Army Tactical Missile Systems, or ATACMS, and precision strike missiles almost exhausted. Around a quarter of the U.S. military’s MQ-9 Reaper drones have also reportedly been lost during the war. Rebuilding these stockpiles will take years.

All of this raises questions about U.S. military readiness and capabilities if Trump chooses to return to war post-election.

The United States still has significant military capabilities in the Middle East, including over 50,000 troops and two aircraft carrier strike groups. Another aircraft carrier strike group is en route and should arrive near the end of this month.

Longer-range and more advanced capabilities like Tomahawk missiles are “significantly depleted,” and Patriot and THAAD batteries are “limited,” but there are “other ways for the president to be able to successfully execute the missions he’s looking at,” Jonathan Panikoff, the senior director of the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council, told Foreign Policy.

“In the short term, the U.S. is likely quite ready to carry out the planned operations,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a senior fellow and director of the defense program at the Center for a New American Security. An additional Patriot unit was sent from Texas to Israel, for instance, and the Pentagon has likely dispersed aircraft and personnel from bases that are very close to Iran and less well defended, such as in Bahrain and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, Pettyjohn said.

But that’s just the short term. The picture could change drastically over a longer time horizon.

“The long-term readiness concerns are quite profound,” Pettyjohn said. These constraints include “munitions stockpiles”—for example, long-range standoff attack missiles and defensive interceptors—“deferred ship maintenance, and disrupted readiness cycles, which affect what forces will be available for future contingencies.”

The U.S. has reportedly told Gulf allies to brace for a short but intense campaign targeting Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, with the goal of strengthening Washington’s negotiation position. But Trump has consistently struggled to dictate the direction of the war, and Iran has proved to be a resilient adversary. The U.S. and Israel conducted thousands of strikes on Iran, but Tehran has not budged in its demands. Iran has also exhibited an ability to quickly adapt its tactics and has proved that even with a diminished military, it can disrupt the flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

“If Iran has prepared for a more protracted campaign of attacks against U.S. forces in the region and civilian infrastructure, that could quickly drain near-term U.S. readiness. So overall, restarting the war would be a huge gamble,” Pettyjohn added.

Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during a recent meeting with commanders reportedly said that Iran’s response would be “immediate, effective” and “without any geographical limitations.” Iran would likely move to strike U.S. bases in the region and energy facilities in Arab countries in response to the war restarting, but it has also signaled that a wider menu of civilian infrastructure could be targeted.

“It is impossible to defend everywhere,” Pettyjohn said. “The U.S. can in the short term surge fighter aircraft to help interdict incoming drones and to potentially suppress Iranian launchers, although the latter must fly over Iran and is at risk of being shot down. But that is a difficult posture to sustain indefinitely as aircraft are likely operating from more distant bases, flying long sorties, and require lots of tanker support.”

Resupplying forces that are under attack with additional weapons would be difficult as well, Pettyjohn said.

The decisions that Trump makes with regard to Iran will also have an impact on U.S. military capabilities in other theaters moving forward. The “more capabilities” that are used against Iran, Panikoff said, “the less that are available for other potential conflicts in the future.”

John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the key issues in the U.S. midterm elections, cyberattacks targeting Russia and Ukraine, and Iran’s proposal to end the war.

Democrats and Republicans made their final pitch to voters on Monday in the run-up to Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Early polling suggests that Democrats will likely win back control of the U.S. House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate in what would be a crushing blow to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement. According to experts, the White House’s poor handling of the Iran war could be to blame.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the key issues in the U.S. midterm elections, cyberattacks targeting Russia and Ukraine, and Iran’s proposal to end the war.

Democrats and Republicans made their final pitch to voters on Monday in the run-up to Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Early polling suggests that Democrats will likely win back control of the U.S. House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate in what would be a crushing blow to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement. According to experts, the White House’s poor handling of the Iran war could be to blame.

In the eight months since U.S. and Israeli forces first launched strikes on Iran, fuel prices have skyrocketed, energy infrastructure has come under fire, and fighting has upended critical supply chains. Products from batteries to medical supplies to sulfur have borne the brunt of the U.S.-Iran war. And the wallets of U.S. voters are far from immune to the fallout.

The cost of living for the average American household has grown by around $2,000 since the war began, according to economists at Moody’s Analytics, or roughly $265 billion for U.S. consumers in total. Coupled with Trump’s continued tariff war with Canada, dissatisfaction with high inflation rates has dropped Trump’s approval rating to 38 percent, per NBC News’s polling average.

Democrats are capitalizing on these figures to try to win control of one or both chambers of Congress. Doing so would give them more leverage to challenge Trump’s foreign-policy agenda, such as by blocking Trump’s national security nominees, cutting off further military funding for the Iran war, investigating alleged corruption within the president’s inner circle, and even trying to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Republicans, meanwhile, tried to distance themselves from Trump’s Iran policies on Monday and instead focused on tried-and-true conservative talking points, such as the need for immigration crackdowns, low taxes, and the (unsubstantiated) threat of Muslim lawmakers in office.

Trump echoed a few of these arguments during a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday. “We have to keep our Congress strong, free, a little bit of apple pie,” Trump said, adding, “We’re not looking to have a jihadist be in our Senate,” in a thinly veiled reference to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is vying to represent Michigan.

Yet Trump spent the bulk of his remarks—originally advertised as a closing midterms campaign speech—discussing topsoil, graffiti stains, piping, algae, limestone, and other construction elements of his capital renovation projects.

It is unclear if these issues will be enough to convince voters to back the Republican Party.

Trump has already vowed to “veto everything” if Democrats take back Congress. In an interview with the New York Post published on Monday, the U.S. president did not rule out issuing preemptive pardons to his aides and allies, such as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company recently came under heavy criticism after the Trump administration reportedly cut off Ukraine from military-grade Starlink internet services. And the administration has already asked the U.S. Supreme Court to temporarily block around 20,000 mail-in ballots from counting in California as part of its growing bid to sow distrust in the U.S. electoral system.

Tuesday, Nov. 3: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung hosts Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni hosts Chilean President José Antonio Kast.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosts Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda.

Wednesday, Nov. 4: Israeli President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party leaders.

Friday, Nov. 5: Chinese President Xi Jinping hosts Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.

Saturday, Nov. 6: New Zealand holds a general election.

Pope Leo XIV begins a multiday trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru

Monday, Nov. 8: Turkey begins hosting the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference.

G-7 foreign ministers hold a two-day meeting in France.

Phony alerts. Residents in Ukraine and Russia received phony emergency alerts late Sunday and early Monday that warned of high radiation levels, chemical threats, ballistic missile attacks, and on-the-ground fighting. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of hacking the Ukrainian emergency alert app and said his country had hacked Russia back in response.

The messages, some of which were riddled with spelling errors, did not appear to worry many locals. However, the cyberattacks did cast new uncertainty over the security of both nations’ emergency alert systems. It also highlighted the very real and ongoing threat of Russian ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine. On Friday, the United States unveiled a $2.1 billion deal to supply 500 more Patriot interceptors to Ukraine; however, sources told Reuters that it could take years for the missiles to arrive, even though Kyiv currently has inadequate air defenses.

This week’s incident occurred just as a limited cease-fire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky expired on Monday. U.S. first lady Melania Trump had negotiated the six-day truce to allow humanitarian aid to reach the devastated city. However, on Monday, Kyiv accused Moscow of using the pause to strengthen its military position in the area. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov responded that any troop movements there were “standard practice” and that Ukraine likely did the same thing.

Last-ditch negotiations. Iran announced a two-day plan on Monday that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States. The deal, which could be implemented within a week, would only occur if Washington agreed to meet Tehran’s seven conditions for ending the war. Those include an end to the U.S. military blockade on Iranian ports, a U.S. waiver on Iranian oil sales, and the cancellation of new U.S. sanctions on Tehran, among other concessions.

“The basis of dialogue ​and talks between Iran and the U.S. via mediators is still Iran’s seven-step proposal, which is now condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said. Trump, however, rejected that deal in September and has since repeatedly threatened to launch fresh strikes on Iran.

“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice,” Trump said on Sunday at a campaign rally. “But at some point, we’re going to have to give them [Iran] the hammer.” Whether such a resumption of fighting will ultimately happen—and if so, when—remains anyone’s guess. Asked on Monday if he’s considering striking Iran after the U.S. midterms, Trump simply said, “No.”

Meanwhile, Persian Gulf nations are preparing themselves for a possible return to heavy fighting, which they expect could trigger Iranian retaliatory strikes on their civilian infrastructure. Alongside deadly Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities, experts fear that the region is not ready to absorb renewed warfare. “Gulf producers spent five decades persuading the world that their supply could withstand regional wars,” Amir Handjani wrote in Foreign Policy. “Eight months of fighting on two fronts have badly weakened that case.”

A win for Moscow? Acting Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova won the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday, making her Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state. According to the Central Election Commission on Monday, Yotova clinched 57.6 percent of the vote, putting her in double digits ahead of former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who secured 39.5 percent. She will be inaugurated on Jan. 22.

Yotova’s win marks a larger victory for the country’s ruling Progressive Bulgaria party. The Russia-friendly group, led by Prime Minister Rumen Radev, secured 131 seats during parliamentary elections in April. Yotova retaining power means that the party’s agenda will now have even less resistance, as Radev and Yotova are united in their support for lifting international sanctions on Moscow as well as their opposition to providing Ukraine with further military assistance.

At the same time, Yotova and Radev have both sought to maintain Bulgaria’s European friendships. Being a member of NATO and the European Union has forced Sofia to exercise a delicate balancing act of fostering closer relations with Russia while also not angering Bulgaria’s traditional allies. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Yotova on her win on Sunday, writing on X, “From security and defence to our competitiveness and energy independence, I look forward to continuing our joint work.”

Four continents, 30 countries, 31,000 miles. English adventurer Karl Bushby completed his 28-year journey around the world on Monday, walking from Punta Arenas, Chile, to his mother’s home in northern England. During that time, he dodged war in the Darién Gap, was airlifted to safety while crossing the Bering Strait, and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel. Visa struggles, the 2008 financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic came close to sapping his resources for good, but the now 57-year-old explorer remained adamant on completing his odyssey entirely on foot. “They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

#6044. Vucic Is Leaving. His Economy Remains.

Q&A: Vucic Is Leaving. His Economy Remains.

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

When President Aleksandar Vucic was defeated in Serbia’s Oct. 25 parliamentary elections, it represented the dramatic end of one of Europe’s most entrenched autocracies. But it also placed a spotlight on the economy that Vucic had built over the past decade in office. Serbia has become reliant on foreign investment from China, among others. His opponents are now hoping to build a more democratic Serbia—one with a closer economic relationship to Europe.

How has Serbia’s economy developed since the 1990s? Was Vucic a successful economic leader of Serbia? What is the student movement’s economic program?

When President Aleksandar Vucic was defeated in Serbia’s Oct. 25 parliamentary elections, it represented the dramatic end of one of Europe’s most entrenched autocracies. But it also placed a spotlight on the economy that Vucic had built over the past decade in office. Serbia has become reliant on foreign investment from China, among others. His opponents are now hoping to build a more democratic Serbia—one with a closer economic relationship to Europe.

How has Serbia’s economy developed since the 1990s? Was Vucic a successful economic leader of Serbia? What is the student movement’s economic program?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: What was Serbia’s strategy for recovering from its 1990s economic collapse in the wake of the breakup of Yugoslavia and the wars that followed? Has it been more reliant on economic integration with Europe or rather direct investment from China and other far-off countries?

Adam Tooze: There’s really no question that Europe is decisive, and the tragedy really of Serbia’s situation since the disastrous end of the Cold War in Yugoslavia—with the bloody wars of the ’90s and then the conflict over Kosovo and Serbia’s isolation—is that it has lost connection to Europe. And so its trajectory has diverged from that of its former Yugoslavia neighbors, Slovenia, Croatia, but also from Hungary, with which, in political terms, you might compare the British regime with [Viktor] Orban in Hungary. I mean, it’s a really tragic story in the sense that Yugoslavia in the late 1980s was one of the relative success stories of Eastern Europe. It was relatively open. It had, you know, regular exchanges, notably with West Germany. It was open to tourism. It was, by the standards of the Eastern Bloc, an open, diverse, cosmopolitan, prosperous, lower-middle-income country. And then as a result of the civil war, and of course Serbia is a key agent in that extremely violent [Slobodan] Milosevic regime, its GDP collapses to about half what it was in the late 1980s by the late 1990s.

And the recovery has been incredibly slow. I find these numbers really hard to believe, having visited Belgrade reasonably recently. But according to the official data, the Serbian GDP per capita didn’t return to its late ’80s levels until the end of the 2010s, in 2018, 2019. The Belgrade I visited, to me, that didn’t fit with those numbers. It seemed like a prosperous, middle-income country now. So it may be that the rest of Serbia is much poorer than the bits of Belgrade that I saw. In any case, it’s that kind of trajectory. And it’s a real outlier within Eastern Europe, even within the former Yugoslavia. Apparently, the Serbians are scandalized by the fact that Montenegro has higher basic pension and minimum wage levels than Serbia today. And China can help in various ways—it can build infrastructure. But for a small country of 6.7 million people who, in every sense, have to clearly be understood as European, to be as isolated as they’ve been, relatively speaking, in political terms and making no progress at all toward any closer serious affiliation with the European Union is a disaster. And in the enthusiasm of the protesters, you sense, of course, the hope that somehow they may finally be able to break out of this disastrous legacy that begins in the early ’90s and is personified by Milosevic and then by Vucic since the early 2010s. It’s a kind of Maidan moment, I think, in that respect. It’s a very dramatic, very dramatic story.

CA: Vucic has earned a reputation in Serbia and elsewhere as a stabilizer of the country, even a modernizer. Was he effective economically?

AT: I mean, as a person, he’s an impressive guy. I’ve been in very small group meetings with him, and he’s a powerhouse. He’s a flyweight boxer. He punches hard. He’s clever. He’s quick on his feet. He knows how to play the Western game. So he’s a bit of a bruiser. He comes out of the ultranationalist scene. So he was, like, doubling down on the hardest, most aggressive Serbian lines in the 1990s. He then does a stint as communications minister as a very young man in his late 20s for Milosevic during the Kosovo conflict, then goes into opposition along with most of the other extreme nationalists after the fall of Milosevic, and then comes back to power after 2008 and rapidly ascends to the position of prime minister. And then in 2015, leverages, I think one has to say, an International Monetary Fund program to build his reputation as the kind of anchor of stability—I mean, Serbia was in terrible trouble financially—and delivers fiscal stability in terms of a falling debt level, which is now down at really low levels, like 45 percent of GDP. It’s much harder for low-income or middle-income countries to kind of carry the kind debt levels that France does, whose debt-to-GDP ratio is about three times that of Serbia or heading that way.

And in that extent, he earns his stripes as an effective manager of the Serbian economy. But the knock is, in a sense, that the tighter their control of fiscal policy and public spending became, the more that gave scope for a discretionary, clientelistic, politically managed regime of investments, of licensing, of crony capitalism, basically, within this tight ship that they were running. So austerity is not, as it were, the opposite of clientelism and crony capitalism, but rather it’s kind of preconditioned that the more tightly you run government spending, the more personal connections to the bosses’ network comes to matter. And this is hardball stuff. You know, I’ve had the privilege of meeting activists in Serbia who’ve had death threats. I mean, this was not an administration or a government to be messed with. And its control of the media, a little bit like in Orban’s Hungary as well, felt, while it was in power, massively solid. So it was a powerful regime of consolidation. And this is something, in fact, that is underrated, I think, as an element of these authoritarian-nationalist projects in Europe in the 2010s. [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, after all, is also notable for having run a very tight fiscal ship. So this kind of logic of politics is a model across Eastern Europe in the former Soviet space.

What Serbian youth understood about politics that their counterparts elsewhere in the West haven’t.

CA: The student movement that has effectively won these elections necessarily comes to power from outside the channels of institutional politics. This was a leaderless, networked, anti-party structure that produced this election outcome. That raises the question of, what does this kind of movement do when it takes power? How does it relate to economic policy and power when it’s handed that opportunity?

AT: Yeah, it’s a really remarkable movement. For those wanting a flavor, I recommend a Guardian article by Aleksandar Matkovic, who was an activist in the movement until he had to leave the country as a result of intimidation by the regime. And it’s a movement that, yeah, we describe it as a student movement. Effectively, it has become a kind of nonparty opposition in a much broader sense. I heard one Serbian commentator say that the remarkable thing about this election is that it has defeated both the regime and its opposition. Because the opposition parties that were living in a kind of live-and-let-live relationship with the government were effectively accepting their fate. And the student movement is singular and radical and novel in saying, “No, there is an alternative for our country.”

They aren’t without a program when it comes to economics. It comes in different forms. So, in early October, there was a platform by 30 leading Serbian economists announcing, first of all, that a victory for the student-led opposition movement would not be a disaster for Serbia. There is a deeply ingrained fear that Serbia could slide back to an era of high inflation, to rapidly depreciating currency. And this was an important statement by some of the leading figures across the academic establishment, former heads of the fiscal council that implemented the austerity drive, people from the University of Belgrade, figures from the central bank, Serbians in exile or working in institutes in Vienna, for instance, all asserting first the bottom line that this is not a vote for economic disaster. And what then has emerged are a variety of different positions of economists and former technocrats who have allied themselves with the movement.

Perhaps the one most commonly mentioned in this context is Dejan Soskic, who between 2010 and 2012, so before Vucic rose to power [in 2014], was the governor of the Serbian National Bank. Now, that’s a period in which the currency was depreciating. So he’s not an entirely uncontroversial figure. But he has emerged since then as a kind of standout centrist figure, arguing essentially for what you would expect—namely, you know, rigorous auditing of government spending, anti-corruption drives, high-quality public spending. It’s not a terribly imaginative kind of policy. But in the Serbian context, it’s important. And his role as a former central bank governor and his insistence that the future will not see further depreciation of the currency, though he considers the possibility of progressive adjustment rather than some sort of collapse so as to increase the competitiveness of the Serbian economy—he’s a kind of anchor figure for that whole issue, which is very neuralgic. How does Serbia revive growth in a conventional framework? How does it overcome corruption? What to do with the currency?

There are also other figures associated with the movement who are offering much more fundamental kind of programs. And one such is Branimir Jovanovic, who is focusing not so much on immediate, short-run issues of governance and central bank policy but on the central issue of growth. How do you get growth going in Serbia other than through exploitative FDI [foreign direct investment] relationships, say with the Chinese, where you always have to ask what’s in it for them, if you like? How could you build a more attractive growth program?

And then there is also what you might call the more genuinely populist left-wing element within the coalition that wants to target Serbian oligarchs, that wants to introduce redistributive taxation, that wants to raise the floor for those who have really suffered through the program of consolidation since the 2010s and to rebuild elements of a welfare state and raise the average standard of living.

So, within this coalition, there are at least those three positions: a kind of clean-hands technocrat that’s concerned about financial markets and the currency, a growth-orientated structural industrial policy kind of person, and a welfarist tax-and-spend program. And it will be, I think, fascinating to see how this is worked out in coming months and years because it’s a central issue for the movement and there isn’t a single coherent platform. But there are a lot of ideas. This is not a movement that’s sort of naive on economic issues, but it’s not one that has consolidated a coherent position.

#6042. AI Is a Choice

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

The Narrow but Feasible Path to Collective Good

Alex Imas, Mohamed A. El-Erian, and James Manyika

Few technologies in history have matched the potential of artificial intelligence to transform the economic landscape in which they emerged. Deployed broadly and effectively, AI can make workers more efficient, enable more dynamic entrepreneurship, and lift economic growth, all of which could be necessary bulwarks against the powerful economic headwinds brought on by aging populations and mounting public debt. AI can also make possible revolutionary new advances in science and medicine and democratize access to knowledge once reserved for the select few.

But the acceleration of AI also carries risks. It could be applied in ways that displace workers, disrupt how students learn, create new bioweapons and cyberweapons, and strain current supplies of energy, water, and land. Compounding these challenges is a mismatch: the benefits of this new technology may take a long time to become visible and widespread. As with earlier transformations, such as the Industrial Revolution, people are likely to experience the disruptions that come from adopting AI before they feel its benefits. And whereas users directly feel the effects of tools like chatbots, some benefits that AI is indirectly making possible, including more accurate predictions of natural disasters and improved medical diagnoses, may not be perceived as owing to the technology at all.

Public opinion has already begun to turn against AI, especially in the United States. One of the main targets has been data centers, with polls showing that a significant majority of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. Opposition to data centers needed for the new AI economy now cuts across party lines and age groups. Numerous surveys have found that residents worry about data centers using too many resources, creating endless noise, and raising their utility bills, all while developers benefit from public subsidies at the communities’ expense.

Although some of these problems are local, they also reflect wider concerns about AI. Some leading figures in AI have no doubt contributed to this anxiety with dramatic warnings of a white-collar-job apocalypse and even the possibility that AI will lead to human extinction. These are real issues that must be understood and addressed, but the growing public pushback against AI also suggests a deeper distributional challenge: individuals, communities, and businesses are being asked to help shepherd a transformative and potentially unsettling new technology at a time when many citizens see its financial gains going to a few people whom they increasingly distrust. AI is now a major issue in American politics: candidates running in competitive elections, no matter which party they belong to, appear increasingly averse to being associated with support for AI.

These anxieties are understandable. AI adoption risks repeating the mistakes of globalization, which generated large and widely spread economic benefits but led to concentrated losses of jobs, growth, and industry in particular communities. Government support in response was insufficient or arrived too late. Although the economy gained overall from free trade, the political bargain failed to give affected workers and communities a credible stake in the gains, even as individuals benefited as consumers from lower prices. The result was a backlash that contributed to the protectionism and fragmentation that continue to plague today’s politics and society.

Turning AI’s capabilities into broadly shared and enduring prosperity requires more than investing in the technology itself. The central challenge of the AI era is coordination and cooperation across groups responsible for the many complementary investments that promote the adoption of AI, including technological diffusion, worker empowerment, firm reorganization, and infrastructure construction. Because these complementary investments must be made across different institutions and at different times, progress requires market mechanisms to encourage cooperation as well as coalitions among organizations, firms, workers, communities, and governments that can turn AI’s technological gains into widespread economic and social benefits. To borrow a concept from game theory, AI is a “cooperative game” in which the largest gains arise only when many groups coordinate, and those gains persist only when every group expects to do better as part of shared coalitions than outside them.

But coalition building requires trust, and public trust—particularly regarding technology and who benefits from it—has eroded. Grand promises of scientific and medical breakthroughs will not overcome deep-seated hostility. Durable cooperation requires giving affected groups a concrete stake in the opportunities and gains that AI generates rather than merely promising future benefits. Without that stake, the individuals and groups whose support is needed to make AI flourish could block its progress. Governments could impose stifling regulations on the industry or stop issuing data center permits, firms could decline to adopt new AI-driven systems, and workers could avoid sharing the tacit knowledge needed to make the technology useful. As the economist and Nobel Prize laureate Michael Spence once observed: “You cannot solve a cooperative game uncooperatively.” The way to ensure that society benefits from AI’s enormous potential while mitigating its risks is to make cooperation the clear choice.

AI is staking a claim to being the next general-purpose technology—one that applies across a wide array of activities, improves over time, and generates complementary innovations. Electricity was an early general-purpose technology. When inventors discovered how to commercially harness electricity in the late nineteenth century, the ability to use it to power many types of machines transformed industrial production. Computing, another general-purpose technology, used electricity to process information itself, revolutionizing sectors as varied as engineering and health care.

But AI works through a more powerful input—intelligence—which makes it possible to interpret information, predict outcomes, diagnose problems, communicate with others, and make decisions. As a result, AI can raise productivity in existing sectors: a nurse can spend less time on paperwork and devote more time to patients, engineers can more quickly develop new designs, and small firms can scale up their analytics capabilities to compete with larger competitors. It can also increase efficiency so significantly that it makes possible wholly new products and services that were otherwise too costly or complicated to deliver.

AI also goes beyond existing general-purpose technologies by transforming the process of research and discovery. By inventing new ways of optimizing scientific processes, AI opens up previously unknown possibilities, similar to what microscopes and telescopes did in earlier eras. AlphaFold, a specialized AI model for which Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared half the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is a clear example. Determining a single protein’s three-dimensional structure from its amino acid sequence used to take months or even years; by using machine learning, AlphaFold has predicted the structures of more than 200 million proteins, fundamentally reshaping what biologists are able to investigate.

The potential of AI is thus a combination of the Industrial Revolution, whose general-purpose technologies transformed production, and the Enlightenment, which brought about inventions for making inventions—the new instruments and new paradigms that transformed the process of discovery. AI holds the promise of providing both the productivity boost and the tools to pave the way for discoveries that can address many of the problems weighing down aging, debt-ridden societies across the world.

The latest wave of AI has diffused at unprecedented speed. Google’s Gemini app and OpenAI’s ChatGPT each now reach more than one billion monthly users. Google’s AI & Economy ATLAS, a study of how people are using the company’s AI products that two of us (Imas and Manyika) worked on, analyzed 15 million interactions in more than 150 countries. It found that AI was used in tasks in 68 percent of occupations, and these occupations made up roughly 90 percent of all U.S. employment. Even automotive technicians and industrial mechanics used AI to interpret test results and diagnose electrical faults. Another study that two of us (Imas and Manyika) ran in collaboration with MIT FutureTech found that nearly half the scientists who were surveyed used some type of AI model every day, saving them time and enabling more interdisciplinary research.

But the gains of diffusion are neither guaranteed nor automatic. AI has been adopted broadly across and within sectors, but thus far its penetration remains fairly shallow. The ATLAS study found that only 21 percent of tasks in a typical occupation have been substantially affected by the technology. According to the Anthropic Economic Index, which measures how the AI model Claude is used in workplace tasks as varied as writing software, analyzing data, and managing administrative workflows, potential use far exceeds actual use. This suggests that access has spread much faster than adoption. Incorporating AI deeply enough to allow it to live up to its potential requires a bigger transformation. A firm does not change how it operates simply by buying access to an AI coding agent. It must also invest in organizational reforms and worker training and often needs to redesign its governance structure or its product lines.

The banking sector, for example, has widely adopted AI but mostly used it to perform superficial tasks. As it is currently deployed, AI gives analysts a faster way to research companies, populate spreadsheets, and identify the sources of investment returns. Deep adoption, on the other hand, requires changing workflows and job responsibilities. A bank must decide what proprietary data to feed a model, how to protect client information, and how to verify the results of the AI models it uses. Junior employees may spend less time collecting information and more time interpreting it, forming ideas, and advising clients. But many tasks that AI can automate are also forms of training. Firms will therefore need to find ways for experienced employees to help younger colleagues acquire the skills the experienced employees once developed by producing the underlying analyses themselves.

The true economic promise of AI lies in deep and transformational adoption. This requires revamping organizational processes, preparing workers to capitalize on the new technology, and applying AI in ways that enhance productivity and innovation and improve consumer welfare. Innovations that increase output and can generate new products and services have not yet appeared at a meaningful scale. But there is enormous latent demand for many new products and services, including specialized services such as individualized tutoring, health care, and legal and financial assistance, and additional demand will emerge from completely new activities that technology will make possible. By fundamentally changing how work is done and what work can be done, AI can lower the cost of providing tailored products, making new opportunities economically viable. Serving demand that previously did not make economic sense adds new value to society rather than merely redistributing a fixed economic pie.

But enlarging the economic pie does not guarantee a smooth transition for every worker. As with globalization, the new demand that AI unlocks will not necessarily arise in the same jobs, sectors, or communities in which existing work is done. This potential mismatch risks major labor market disruption and political backlash. Public anxiety is already growing, especially among younger workers seeking entry-level positions that are the most likely to be automated by AI. One study by the Stanford economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen found that the employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in occupations most exposed to AI automation was 19 percent lower than it would have been if employment had grown at the same rate as occupations less exposed to AI disruption. Yet the overall effect of AI on jobs, including entry-level positions, remains uncertain. The Economist has estimated that AI has created around one million jobs in the United States but led to about 200,000 layoffs, and the gap between the unemployment rate among 20-to-24-year-olds and the overall unemployment rate is low compared with recent decades. Most likely, as one of us (Manyika) wrote with Spence in these pages, in 2023, some jobs will be lost, some will be gained, and many more will be permanently changed.

Harnessing AI’s potential to increase prosperity without destabilizing society requires coordination. In addition to AI companies making new models, products, and tools, infrastructure developers must build the physical systems such as data centers that underpin AI. Businesses need to supply data and drive the organizational transformation to deploy models at their full potential—not just for efficiency but also to expand existing products and services or create new ones. Employers must decide how these technologies will be used, how workflows will be transformed, and how to enable workers to be more productive. Workers have to adopt the technology and invest in learning AI-relevant skills. Local communities must provide the land for data centers and consent to the technology’s expansion. And governments need to set rules, fund foundational research, and provide social insurance to support and manage transitions for those whose work or livelihoods are displaced by AI.

Each of these groups bears unique costs, captures different shares of the benefits, answers to its own constituencies, and responds to distinct incentives. This also means that unless they coordinate—whether through market mechanisms or active cooperation—these groups could slow or block AI development. Firms might underinvest in organizational change and use AI only to cut costs rather than to expand revenues, workers might resist or slow down adoption, communities might block infrastructure, and governments might restrict development. Each action might make sense in isolation, but together they lead to a suboptimal outcome for society.

This is a classic cooperative game scenario in game theory: these groups can accomplish much more when they work in concert than when they act individually and without coordination. A coalition with a common goal does not need to be a formal organization; it can be any grouping of actors who operate in ways that allow them to coordinate decisions and contribute resources to a shared project through contracts, policies, standards, investment commitments, or political bargains. Each possible coalition can generate more growth and economic value by promoting the adoption and diffusion of AI than any one actor can by operating separately.

In an ideal world, all these actors would form a single “grand coalition” to capture as much value from AI as possible. Their complementary actions and active coordination to promote AI would kick off a virtuous cycle in which wider adoption would spur advancements that would make AI more useful for society, unlock new demand and productivity growth, and encourage more people, communities, and companies to adopt the technology and support its expansion.

Such a grand coalition, however, is a benchmark rather than a blueprint. Progress is not all or nothing; smaller, more focused coalitions can still create economic and social gains that far outweigh what each actor could achieve alone. What is needed is a stable coalition—one in which no participant or group of participants can do better by leaving and doing something on their own. In the AI economy, exiting the coalition does not mean building a rival AI system. It simply means exercising a veto on increased AI use, which could take the form of imposing a local moratorium on data centers, resisting workplace adoption of AI, or blocking new regulations that encourage AI development. Because the withdrawal of any one participant would destroy more value than that participant could ever capture alone, it is critical that every essential group prefers being inside the coalition to being outside it.

A crucial question, then, is how to share the gains of working together so that cooperation remains stable over time and no coalition member wants to leave. In the case of AI, one factor that can help drive cooperation is that the technology creates conditions for what economists call a “convex game”: because the inputs to AI are complementary, each new participant makes everyone else’s contribution more valuable, causing the gains from joining the coalition to increase at an accelerating rate. Building better computing infrastructure, for instance, makes AI models and tools more capable; more capable models and tools increase the benefits for companies that want to invest in transforming their organizational processes and retraining workers, which increases productivity and spurs innovation; and wider adoption of AI in the workplace drives the need for additional computing power, which creates incentives for more infrastructure providers to build. Once a core group starts working together, the next actor that wants to join has even more to gain.

Prices, contracts, and incentives are indispensable for building a stable coalition, and market design and competition provide the architecture that enables coordination. But markets alone will not be enough. In the case of AI, the various costs and benefits will not unfold on the same timelines for all participants; some of them will benefit long before others catch up. Public institutions are necessary. Only policymakers, for instance, can create the common rules that will allow frontier labs in the coalition to coordinate on making AI safer, and only policymakers can provide enough support for workers to adapt to the AI economy. The bitter experiences that many workers and communities felt during globalization have made coalition building harder yet even more necessary.

A workable coalition does not need to bring every participant to the same negotiating table. A national bargain can establish common terms and align incentives on issues such as AI safety standards, workforce transition support, and infrastructure permitting, and smaller agreements at workplaces and in local communities can bring needed groups on board to cooperate. At both levels, the principle is the same: each group must receive a credible stake in the upside of the economic gains that the coalition creates through the overall growth of AI.

At the national level, cooperation should focus on the groups whose participation will determine whether AI technology can scale enough to generate massive economic gains. This includes the federal government, leading labs, major infrastructure builders and providers, organized labor, and large firms deploying AI. Big business matters because its use of technology and its investments in the workforce create demand that fuels the entire supply chain. Labor organizations will want to negotiate favorable terms for workforce transition, such as expanded unemployment and wage insurance, as well as for retraining; a lack of participation from organized labor will deprive the coalition of the support needed to facilitate adoption, especially in sectors such as construction in which unions have more power. For critical infrastructure, including power grids, telecommunications networks, and payment systems, the priority needs to be cybersecurity and reliability: before they integrate AI deeply into core operations, infrastructure providers need to believe that more capable models will not expose them to catastrophic risk.

The government can establish a predictable, risk-based regulatory framework to set clear standards in potentially dangerous areas such as biosecurity and to help coordinate the testing of advanced AI systems. A national framework would preempt a fragmented patchwork of idiosyncratic state-by-state bans on low-risk commercial uses of AI. Policymakers can also support AI development by funding research on foundational questions in artificial intelligence and increasing immigration and visa pathways for highly skilled workers to attract top global talent to U.S. labs. AI model and application developers, meanwhile, can participate in safety testing, and companies building out AI capacity can make available more computing power to small businesses, nonprofits, and local governments. Infrastructure providers can construct new data centers and show their support for the communities they work in by implementing ratepayer protections and paying local taxes, and large companies can invest in worker training, organizational transformation, and new business models. Finally, organized labor can supply the skilled employees needed to build the physical infrastructure underlying AI adoption, help redesign organizational workflows within companies, and lend its political weight to promoting AI nationally.

Each group benefits more than it is expected to contribute. AI model and application developers and infrastructure providers gain a predictable development path and a skilled workforce. Large firms have access to the support they need to more deeply adopt AI and improve their productivity. Workers gain new opportunities and job security during the economic transition. Washington also stands to benefit as the economy grows and the United States maintains its global technological leadership.

AI model developers and other companies in the AI ecosystem are already working together to diffuse AI more widely. Leading developers, including Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, along with partner organizations, have embedded engineers inside large organizations to identify valuable uses of AI, redesign workflows, and integrate new technology systems into production. These efforts recognize that model access is not enough: adoption requires technical assistance, organizational knowledge, and sustained engagement. A coalition can extend this capacity to smaller firms, schools, clinics, and municipalities. For AI model and application developers, supporting diffusion expands the market and provides insurance against potential political backlash. Only if the gains of AI adoption are shared with a broad swath of organizations and the general public will citizens support the expansion of the technology in society.

Frameworks for coalition building with labor groups are also emerging. Rather than working with individual firms to sign bespoke agreements, technology developers, industry associations, and policymakers are supporting worker cooperation through existing unions, apprenticeships, and retraining programs. The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, for example, is mobilizing its members to oppose data center moratoriums while calling for better labor agreements. Google is working with the IBEW’s partner organizations to train 100,000 electrical workers and 30,000 apprentices, giving workers access to well-paid jobs and providing developers with a source of skilled labor and the political support needed to build.

At the local level, new data centers may impose concentrated costs on communities even when they create national benefits for AI users. Developers should therefore negotiate agreements that protect ratepayers and provide tangible benefits for communities through increased local revenue, better infrastructure, and more employment opportunities. Templates for how to do this are taking shape in many U.S. states. Leading AI companies and “hyperscalers,” including Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, have signed on to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary commitment to pay the full cost of new power generation and grid upgrades in areas where they are building data centers so that household electricity bills do not rise. These companies are also funding local workforce programs and water-restoration projects and contributing property tax revenue that will allow communities to pay for new schools and roads.

The economic benefits that AI brings will increase the stability of emerging coalitions as long as they are shared. The distribution of benefits does not need to be equal, but for groups providing complementary inputs, benefits must be apportioned according to what each group contributes and also be adjusted as the technology evolves. In practice, determining each group’s contribution is not an exact science but an ongoing structured negotiation: tools such as utility tariffs, labor agreements, and enabling policies can allocate benefits in ways that reflect the role of different groups in supporting AI expansion and adoption. The share of the upside that each coalition member receives must be large enough to make participation more attractive than obstruction. Giving key players a real stake in the economic surplus that is generated is how those who might have been potential impediments to AI become participants in, and perhaps even advocates for, the expanded use of this new technology.

Where AI substitutes for existing tasks rather than complementing them, policymakers can also learn from what went wrong with globalization. Public programs to help displaced workers can be effective, but they must be accessible enough to provide support when technological disruption occurs. Targeted parts of the federal government’s Trade Adjustment Assistance program to compensate and retrain workers affected by globalization succeeded where they were put in place—research by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that eligibility for wage insurance under the program increased reemployment, shortened the amount of time out of work, and raised cumulative earnings—but it reached only a small portion of workers. Other research found that most support was provided through disability benefits that required workers to permanently exit the labor force. With AI, policymakers will need to set up expanded wage and unemployment insurance programs and support employer-led retraining programs that help workers transition into in-demand roles before displacement occurs rather than improvise after workers begin to suffer.

A coalition does not need to be built all at once. Cooperation should start in areas in which complementary benefits are clearest and participation constraints are easiest to identify, including promoting AI adoption and worker training in particular sectors such as health care or skilled trades, and encouraging support for new data centers. At the national level, safety cooperation can grow out of partnerships between coalitions and the government. Because AI’s development trajectory remains uncertain, cooperation agreements should center on investments that could pay out across multiple plausible scenarios and can be revised as the trajectory of AI becomes clearer.

International cooperation can grow in the same way. Although AI may well eventually require cooperation among adversaries and allies alike, Washington can start by forming a U.S.-led coalition built around trusted partners willing to accept common safety and security standards. The United States could, for example, set up a coalition among trusted partners that agrees on principles and frameworks in exchange for access to technology and cooperation. This coalition will naturally widen as its terms prove workable and more countries see the benefits of participating. It could eventually include China, which, given its advanced AI capabilities, is critical to addressing AI safety issues; this will require navigating complex questions of alignment and verification, however, including how to set up trusted validation bodies and mechanisms.

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision provides an instructive example of international cooperation. It began in 1974 as a small forum among national regulators in 12 advanced industrialized countries and over time developed common standards for how to supervise banks around the world without empowering an imposing supranational authority, expanding its scope as those standards proved valuable. The Basel Committee was the seed for what is now the dominant international architecture that identifies and minimizes the risks of financial instability, including setting standards for how much capital banks need to hold and how to classify the riskiness of securities held on banks’ balance sheets. A future coalition for AI standards could grow through the same combination of clear entry conditions and credible commitments that have made the Basel Committee and the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes voluntary technical standards, successful.

Harnessing the potential of AI will not be easy. Critics will immediately jump to the conclusion that there are many reasons why such coalitions will not work in practice. Labs might decide that they can earn more on their own, incumbent firms might try to convert cooperation into tools to protect their market share, and governments might promise support for workers and communities and fail to deliver, as was the case with globalization.

But there is reason to be cautiously optimistic about cooperation in the age of AI. Because the technology is still relatively early in its development, it is possible to identify the groups needed to initiate cooperation, and labs, governments, communities, employers, and labor organizations have already shown interest in different parts of the bargain. Ultimately, society does not need to choose between innovation and shared prosperity. The two can be complements: cooperation will drive growth, and sharing the gains of such growth will sustain the cooperation needed to keep it going.

ALEX IMAS is Director of AGI Economics at Google DeepMind and Roger L. and Rachel M. Goetz Professor of Behavioral Science, Economics, and Applied AI at the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business.

MOHAMED A. EL-ERIAN is Rene M. Kern Professor of Practice at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, Chief Economic Adviser at Allianz, and Chair of the Board of Directors of the Center for Global Development.

JAMES MANYIKA is Senior Vice President at Google Alphabet and its President of Research, Labs, Technology, and Society. He is a Distinguished Fellow at Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute and a Visiting Professor at the University of Oxford’s Blavatnik School of Government.

#6041. In California’s Central Valley, Democrats hope to harvest fruits of Proposition 50

By Sean Campbell, Nicholas Corral, Jules Cox, Aden Max Juarez, Caitlin Roehmholdt, Jose Trejo and Maybeline Tucker

BAKERSFIELD, Calif. — In a final get-out-the-vote push Monday, California’s two U.S. senators joined Randy Villegas at a labor union headquarters in the Central Valley district that could be critical to Democrats’ attempts to win back control of the House.

The 22nd District, spanning farmland from north of Fresno to south of Bakersfield, was redrawn via Proposition 50 to weaken six-term Republican Rep. David Valadao’s chance of reelection.

Valadao, who lost his seat once in 2018 during a Democratic takeover in President Donald Trump’s first term, is facing an even tougher environment now thanks to redistricting, high prices and the war in Iran. Inside Elections lists the race as a Toss-up.

“This is still very much a battleground district for California and for the country,” Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla told reporters after the rally Monday morning. “That’s why you see the level of commitment from so many volunteers knocking on doors, making the phone calls, getting out the vote.”

Valadao has defied the odds before. He won the seat back in 2020 after losing by less than 1,000 votes in 2018 and has held it since. He is the only congressional Republican who voted to impeach Trump in 2021 who is still serving in the House. Trump won the counties in the 22nd District in 2024, but under the new lines, the district would only have gone for Trump by 1.5 percentage points, one reason why party and labor leaders made the trip Monday in a final push.

Villegas, a mechanic and progressive college professor, wore Converse and cheered as speaker after speaker proclaimed he would be the winner once votes are counted in California.

Introducing himself as the Robin to Padilla’s Batman, Democratic Sen. Adam B. Schiff said Californians “need a champion like Randy in Congress.” He egged on the crowd: “Are you so over David Valadao?”

Padilla, center, and Schiff, right, campaigned for Villegas on Monday. (USC Annenberg Media)

The senators are not the only big names to stump in the district. In September and October, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., as well as House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., appeared in the Central Valley. When asked, Villegas pushed back against the notion that his race was only competitive because of the favorably redrawn district.

“This is a district that we would’ve been competitive in regardless,” Villegas told reporters after the morning canvass kickoff. “Our message is one that has resonated across the political spectrum.”

Addressing the crowd in both English and Spanish, Villegas dropped a few curse words to punctuate his get-out-the-vote messaging. He told the labor activists gathered in the standing-room-only rally that when their sunscreen and sweat dripped in their eyes while canvassing later, they should remember, “That is the pain David Valadao and Republicans are going to be feeling.”

Cathy Abernathy, a Republican consultant and prominent GOP activist in Bakersfield, said Villegas is “too far” left for the Central Valley, but she stopped short of saying she was confident Valadao could win. She also criticized Prop 50 and the way Democrats redrew the lines to break up cities and counties and said she would support national reform of the redistricting process.

“David Valadao, he’s resilient. He’s a fighter. He has constantly gone against the odds,” said Matthew Martin, chair of the Kern County Young Republicans, taking a moment to chat with reporters after sending get-out-the-vote text messages in the Republican Party headquarters in Bakersfield. If it wasn’t for Prop 50 shifting the makeup of the district so dramatically, “I think this would be more of a slam dunk for David Valadao,” he said.

Martin predicted that Latinos age 45 and under would be the deciding factor in the election. The district is 74 percent Latino, according to 2020 Census data.

Prop 50, pushed by Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom and approved by voters last year, 64 percent to 36 percent, redrew the 22nd to make it easier for a Democrat to win. Valadao’s own home base of Hanford, where his family owns a dairy farm, was carved out of his district.

Valadao posted a photo of himself on Facebook dropping his ballot in a drop box in Hanford. His campaign did not respond to multiple requests from reporters seeking to cover activity on the ground.

Instead, Valadao joined California Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton at a rally last Thursday. He also posted on his Facebook page about celebrating the birthday of the founder of the Sikh religion, Guru Nanak. At the event with Johnson last month, the congressman said, “We’ve got a lot on the line. We’ve got to keep fighting all the way towards the end.”

The district is at the epicenter of multiple nationwide fights: It saw early immigration enforcement raids during Trump’s second term, and changes to Medicaid through the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” are expected to have a major impact. Roughly six in 10 residents in the district are enrolled in the state’s Medicaid program, known in California as Medi-Cal.

For Republican voter Kevin Caid, Trump was top of mind as he dropped off his ballot at California State University, Bakersfield. He lives in the neighboring district represented by Republican Rep. Vince Fong. Caid voted Republican down the ballot, saying his top issues were taxes and keeping a nuclear weapon out of Iranian hands.

“If gas is high, you know, that’s the price it takes,” Caid said.

Linda Fiddler, a canvasser for the Villegas campaign, is a long-time campaign volunteer in the district, having worked on Democratic campaigns since 2010. She described Villegas as a “game changer” compared to previous Democratic candidates.

“They never distinguished themselves from the Republican,” Fiddler said. She attributes Valadao’s previous success to voters lacking a strong reason to vote against him. She hopes Villegas’ messaging of “you deserve more” is that reason.

Jacob Brunell, 28, the field director for the Westside Democratic Headquarters, said he’s canvassed multiple times in Bakersfield, but this time he felt the excitement and noticed Republican voters crossing party lines.

“This is an area that has been consistently, throughout time, screwed over by land developers, by energy owners,” Brunell said. “I think [voters] are happy to see a Bernie Sanders-backed progressive taking on this fight and hopefully winning the election.”

Bakersfield Vice Mayor Manpreet Kaur said that in this land of farm workers, she has seen young people turning out to vote at the same level as voters aged 60 to 65, and said she believes it is to protect their immigrant families.

“Children of immigrants are becoming that protective barrier between Trump’s illegal operations being carried out and harming our families and our communities,” Kaur said. “The immigrant struggle is everyone’s struggle, whether they admit it or not.”

Jon Rodriguez, 26, a Latino voter from Bakersfield, said immigration was the biggest issue driving his vote after Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity increased in East Bakersfield. While he lives in the bordering 20th District, represented by Fong and packed with more Republicans by Prop 50, Rodriguez said he would have voted for Villegas if he could have.

“Whether they’re citizens or noncitizens, whether they have a visa here or they have full-time citizenship, they’re still scared because they know by the color of their skin they’re going to be targeted,” Rodriguez said after dropping off his ballot at a voting station at California State University, Bakersfield.

Andres Ramirez, 21, of Bakersfield, said he voted for Villegas. Because his parents are in the process of applying for U.S. citizenship, he said he hopes having Democrats in office will protect them from being deported.

“With Trump, he’s wanting to deport us,” Ramirez said. “But I’m legal here, so I make sure that he doesn’t want to, like, attack us.”

Democrats have focused their attack ads on Valadao’s vote for Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which imposed a work requirement for Medicaid eligibility. Cecilia Torres, 30, cited that vote as she cast her ballot at CSU Bakersfield.

“I do kind of fear for my health care, and will it be affordable? Will I have it, even?” Torres said. “I really hope to see him removed from office and never again see him on the ballot.”

Dolores Huerta, a liberal labor icon who endorsed Villegas in the primary, died in Bakersfield last week at age 96. Chants of “Sí se puede,” a phrase coined by Huerta meaning, “Yes, we can,” broke out during Villegas’ Monday morning rally.

“It is everything,” Villegas said when asked what Huerta’s legacy meant to him. “One thing that I’ll always take to heart is her own words: that every moment is a potential organizing opportunity, every person is a potential activist, and every minute is a chance to change the world.”

This story was reported from Texas by students from the University of Southern California Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism. Direct questions to christina.bellantoni@usc.edu

#6039. Iran Is Talking Peace but Preparing for War

Analysis: Iran Is Talking Peace but Preparing for War
